youtube.baslik: Auditory Steady-State Response (ASSR) | Lesson 198 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
What is the ASSR, and why does the modulation frequency matter? In this lesson we cover the amplitude-modulated stimulus, statistical detection of the response, 80 to 100 Hz modulation in sleep and about 40 Hz in awake adults, multiple-frequency testing, and how ASSR compares with tone burst ABR, including its limitations.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Hall, New Handbook of Auditory Evoked Responses; Picton, Human Auditory Evoked Potentials; Katz, Handbook of Clinical Audiology; Joint Committee on Infant Hearing, Year 2019 Position Statement.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

sahneler.alt: Modulated sound, statistical detection, frequency-specific thresholds
cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn about the auditory steady-state response, or ASSR, in detail.
We will cover modulation frequency, multiple-frequency testing, and how ASSR differs from the auditory brainstem response, or ABR.
The auditory steady-state response is a rhythmic response in the brain to a sound that changes continuously and regularly.
The stimulus is a tone at a certain frequency; this is called the carrier frequency.
The amplitude of the tone is raised and lowered a set number of times per second; this is called amplitude modulation.
How many times per second the amplitude rises and falls is the modulation frequency; in this example, eighty hertz.
The carrier frequency sets which region of the cochlea is stimulated; in other words, it is the frequency being tested.
The auditory pathway follows this rhythm, and brain electrical activity shows a response at the same rate, the modulation frequency.
In short, the carrier tells us what we are testing, and the modulation frequency tells us where to look for the response.
In ASSR, the response is not found by eye from wave peaks as in ABR; it is looked for in the frequency domain.
The recorded brain activity is broken down into its frequency components with a Fourier transform.
In the graph, the gray bars show random electrical noise at the frequencies around the modulation frequency.
If the stimulus is heard, a peak clearly above the noise appears exactly at the modulation frequency.
The system uses a statistical test to check whether this peak is significantly larger than the noise at neighboring frequencies.
Some systems instead look at how consistent the phase of the response is across repetitions.
Because statistics decides whether a response is present, interpretation depends less on the clinician's experience in picking waves.
The setup is like ABR; electrodes are placed on the scalp as we saw in the lesson on electrode placement.
An infant is in natural sleep; an adult lies in a comfortable chair, eyes closed and muscles relaxed.
As recording continues, random noise averages down, and small responses become statistically detectable.
The system stops the recording at that level once the response is significant or a preset maximum time runs out.
The level is then lowered step by step to find the level at which the response can no longer be detected.
Total time depends on the infant's sleep, the noise and the degree of loss; deep, calm sleep shortens the test markedly.
Which part of the auditory pathway generates the ASSR depends on the modulation frequency.
With modulation around forty hertz, the response comes mainly from the thalamus and auditory cortex, and it is large in awake adults.
But this response shrinks markedly in sleep and under sedation, and it cannot be recorded reliably in infants.
So forty hertz ASSR can be used to estimate thresholds in awake, calm adults.
With modulation between eighty and one hundred hertz, the response comes mainly from the brainstem.
This response is barely affected by sleep or sedation, so it is the ASSR used in infants and sleeping children.
In the clinic, ASSR in infant and child assessment usually means this high modulation frequency response.
The simplest stimulus is the amplitude-modulated tone we have seen.
The frequency of the tone can also be moved slightly up and down at a regular rate; this is called frequency modulation.
When amplitude and frequency modulation are applied together, as mixed modulation, the response is usually larger.
Some newer systems use chirp-based stimuli for each frequency band to increase response amplitude.
Whatever the stimulus, the principle is the same: the carrier sets the test frequency, and the modulation sets the response frequency.
ASSR can also be given with a bone vibrator, but the usable intensity range by bone conduction is narrower.
One of the main advantages of ASSR is that several frequencies and both ears can be tested at the same time.
To do this, each carrier frequency is modulated at a different modulation frequency, between about seventy seven and one hundred five hertz.
For example, the right ear carriers at five hundred, one thousand, two thousand and four thousand hertz each have their own modulation rate.
The left ear carriers get slightly different modulation rates, so eight stimuli can be presented at once.
Each modulation frequency in the recording works like a label showing which ear and carrier it belongs to.
This method can shorten the test markedly compared with testing frequencies one by one.
But when many stimuli are presented together, individual response amplitudes may be somewhat smaller.
At high intensities the stimuli can interact in the cochlea, so in some cases frequencies are tested separately.
In the clinic, the main purpose of ASSR is to estimate frequency-specific thresholds in people who cannot do behavioral testing.
In this example, the blue dashed line shows the lowest level at which an ASSR response was obtained at each frequency.
The ASSR threshold is not identical to the behavioral threshold; the difference is accounted for with a correction value.

cumleler.yazi: The corrected value is reported as an estimated hearing level, in eHL.
cumleler.ses: The corrected value is reported as an estimated hearing level, in E H L.

cumleler: The difference is usually larger with normal hearing and mild loss, and smaller with severe loss.
Because correction values vary with the equipment, stimulus and age, each clinic follows the values recommended for its system.
In infants, results are confirmed with behavioral audiometry as the child grows.

maddeler.metin: Residual hearing: aid and implant decisions
_Extra information_ when tone burst ABR absent

cumleler: Because it uses a continuous tone, ASSR can reach higher levels than brief tone burst stimuli.
Depending on the system, testing is possible at levels close to one hundred twenty decibels HL.
This helps separate severe from profound hearing loss.
The amount of residual hearing is important for hearing aid fitting and cochlear implant assessment.
So in infants whose tone burst ABR shows no response at the equipment limit, ASSR provides complementary information.
If a response at a frequency appears only at a very high level, the residual hearing result is weighed together with other tests.
But the risk of measurement error also rises at such high levels; we will see this under limitations.
In ABR, an experienced clinician decides whether a response is present by looking at the waveform; in ASSR, a statistical test decides.
In tone burst ABR, frequencies are usually tested in turn; in ASSR, several frequencies can be tested at once.
Because ASSR can reach higher levels, it offers a wider measurement range in profound loss.
In ABR, wave latencies and morphology are assessed; ASSR only tells whether a response is present and how large it is.
So ASSR does not assess the synchronous firing of nerve fibers, that is, neural synchrony.
With normal hearing and mild loss, tone burst ABR is generally considered more accurate for threshold estimation.
Like every method, ASSR has limitations to keep in mind.
At very high air-conduction levels and with bone-conduction stimuli, electrical artifact can look like a real response.
In auditory neuropathy, ASSR thresholds may not reflect true hearing, so they are read together with ABR and the cochlear microphonic.
In an awake, moving or tense infant, residual noise rises and the test runs longer or ends without a result.
With normal hearing and mild loss, the estimate carries a wider margin of error.
Because it gives no latency information, ASSR does not replace the neurological ABR when looking for a retrocochlear problem.
In infant assessment, ASSR is not used alone but as part of a test battery.
First the middle ear and otoacoustic emissions, or OAEs, are assessed; click ABR is used to look for auditory neuropathy.
In most protocols, tone burst ABR is the basis of frequency-specific threshold estimation.
ASSR is added especially in severe loss, when tone burst ABR shows no response, or to shorten testing time.
As the child grows, all these estimates are confirmed with behavioral audiometry, and the hearing aid settings are updated.

sahneler.metin: Be cautious with ASSR responses seen only at very high levels or by bone conduction, at low frequencies; compare with ABR and other findings.
cumleler: A tip from the field: in an infant with profound loss, be wary of an ASSR response seen only at the highest levels and low frequencies.
At these levels electrical artifact can look like a real response; by bone conduction this risk starts at lower levels.
Compare the result with tone burst ABR, the cochlear microphonic and the history; if there is a mismatch, repeat the test.
Always state the modulation frequency, the stimulus type and the correction method in the report.
ASSR is a rhythmic brain response, at the modulation frequency, to a continuous sound whose amplitude or frequency is modulated.
Forty hertz can be used in awake adults; in infants and sleeping people, modulation between eighty and one hundred hertz is used.
Several frequencies and both ears can be tested at once, and a statistical test decides whether a response is present.
ASSR gives valuable information in severe loss, but it carries no latency information and does not replace ABR.

sahneler.soru: Which modulation frequency in a sleeping infant?
sahneler.aciklama: The high-rate response from the _brainstem_ is barely affected by sleep.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: which modulation frequency range is used for ASSR in a sleeping infant?

cumleler: The correct answer is C: between eighty and one hundred hertz.
The response in this range comes mainly from the brainstem and is preserved in sleep; the forty hertz response shrinks markedly in sleep.
